Parton. Partons are the generic name for quarks and gluons that constitute hadrons, used when their exact identity or behavior within high-momentum-transfer interactions is being considered. The parton model, developed to explain deep inelastic scattering, treats hadrons as collections of point-like constituents that carry fractions of the hadron's momentum. Parton distribution functions quantify the probability of finding each parton type at a given momentum fraction.

The parton model emerged from Bjorken scaling, the surprising observation that deep inelastic scattering rates depend only on a dimensionless ratio. This revealed hadrons' internal compositeness and vindicated the quark model quantitatively. Modern parton distribution functions, refined from thousands of experiments, are essential for predicting cross-sections at the Large Hadron Collider and remain central to precision tests of the Standard Model.

Partons include both valence partons and sea partons. Valence partons are the quarks that define hadron quantum numbers—a proton contains two up quarks and one down quark. Sea partons are transient quark-antiquark pairs and gluons generated by quantum fluctuations. Collectively, all partons carry one hundred percent of the hadron's momentum. At high momentum fractions, above ten percent, valence partons dominate. At low momentum fractions, below one percent, gluon splitting takes over. The parton model shows how quarks are parton species within hadrons, and how gluons are parton species that carry momentum via quantum chromodynamics, all while protons remain the most studied parton system.
